newsitem.title: UK: Britain's builders set for 3 yrs growth ahead - report.
newsitem.headline: Britain's builders set for 3 yrs growth ahead - report.

text.p: Britain's building sector received fresh evidence that it is back on track on Monday after an industry survey predicted growth for the next three years thanks to a rebound in housing and commercial property demand.

Total construction output growth is set to increase from 0.9 percent in 1996 to around two percent in 1997, a further three percent in 1998 before slowing down to two percent growth in 1999 according to a three-year outlook from the Building Material Producers (BMP) group.
The news backed up the rosy outlook painted in a spate of recent British building sector corporate results after five years of recession which cost the country half a million jobs.
Charles Novotny, chairman of the BMP Forecast Panel, welcomed the news which comes in face of severe cutbacks in public infrastructure spending.

"Despite our disappointment at the declining levels of public investment in construction projects, we are pleased that the industry is well placed to accommodate the new opportunities provided by the private sector," he said.
New private housing starts are seen hitting 160,000 this year, rising to 165,000 in 1998 and dropping to 160,000 the year after. That compares with 145,400 in 1996.
Alan Wilen, BMP economist told a press briefing that the growth is concentrated in the south east of England but that this should broaden out this year in a "ripple-effect".
That verdict has also been voiced by companies with house building activities like Amec Plc.
AMEX Group Chief Executive Peter Mason told an industry lunch last week that the housing recovery should soon spread.
Most of the growth in housing starts comes from the private sector while public housing remains on the decline because of cutbacks in government spending.

Commercial property activity is seen growing by 8.5 percent this year, eight percent next year and 5.5 percent in 1999, fuelled by retail development and double-digit growth in the entertainment sector.

"The entertainment sector has seen the most spectacular growth due to money from the (National) Lottery, Millennium projects and things like football clubs investing in their ground facilities," Wilen said
"Nineteen ninety seven should see this sector increase by 19 percent and 17 percent in 1998 before trailing off to 12 percent in 1999," he said.
But there are some black spots for the industry. Most notable is infrastructure which has suffered from reduced road spending.
Its outlook remains erratic, with output seen falling from 4.3 percent in 1996 to three percent in 1997. In 1998 it is seen up four percent, but falling back to two percent by 1999.
BMP said it had factored in the impact of a windfall tax being levied by the opposition Labour Party if it wins the May 1 election.
"Should Labour get into office their proposed windfall tax could have a dampening effect on investment by the privatised utilities," the BMP survey said.
Industrial spending on facilities like new factories is seen growing from 0.1 percent last year to three percent in 1997 and 1998, tailing off to two percent in 1999.
